paras: The expulsion of John Johnson from Decatur, Indiana, occurred on Friday evening, July 3, 1903, when a mob attacked a Black man from Wren, Ohio, who had come to town to trade, and chased him out. Two policemen clubbed members of the mob and saw Johnson off by the Erie railroad, but the mob achieved its purpose of banishing him. The only person punished, Will Foreman, was fined one dollar and costs, a sentence carried by wire across the country and called "a travesty of justice" by the Indianapolis Journal.

The Indianapolis Journal described Decatur as a town where residents had boasted since the Civil War that "no nigger can live here." According to the Journal, an "inoffensive negro" had been "run out" a year earlier, and the wire called the 1903 attack "the second race riot here during the last year."

The fullest account, credited to a Decatur "Journal" and reprinted in the Berne Witness, said men who "hate the niggers" spotted the visitor and organized a "gang" to run him out. He did his trading "in a quiet manner," then went into a saloon where the mob was organizing and bought drinks for the crowd. As he started to leave he was grabbed, and he resisted.

Night policeman Mangold pushed through the crowd and clubbed the man holding Johnson so that "the rioter was nearly floored." Johnson broke loose and ran south on Second street with the mob behind him, was caught again in a clothing store, and broke away a second time. With Mangold and a second policeman, Cordua, he went to the Erie railroad and started home. The wire put the mob at 100 and said several citizens were badly beaten by the officers' clubs; no injury to Johnson is reported.

On Mangold's affidavit, Mayor Coffee fined Foreman one dollar and costs for assault and battery, the costs given as $9.80 by the Indianapolis Journal. The mayor reprimanded Foreman and others, declaring that "this man has the same right in Decatur as any other American citizen." Foreman was the only person arrested.

Leading citizens hoped Johnson would return and swear affidavits charging the mob with inciting a riot, and business men promised to seek every member's arrest. No report of further arrests or riot charges appears in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Journal noted the attack among state news on July 6 and devoted an editorial, "Civilization in Decatur," to it the same day. The editorial called it "a disgrace to our civilization" and urged the state to pursue the mob as it had "whitecap outrages and lynchings." Its July 8 follow-up was headed "Decatur Negro Baiter Is Fined One Dollar and Costs," and the Berne Witness headed its account "Another Negro Run Down in Decatur."

Two wire stories carried it beyond Indiana. The first, "Some Good Citizens Have Headaches," called Johnson "a respected citizen of Wren" and ran in the Rock Island Argus and the Plymouth Tribune. The second reported that "public indignation here against the negro" had grown over Foreman's one-dollar fine; it ran as "Decatur, Ind., Has the Disease" in Montgomery and "Leader of a Negro Mob" in Oxford, Mississippi. It also appeared in Birmingham, Salt Lake City and Beatrice, Nebraska, and the Wisconsin Tobacco Reporter dropped "against the negro" and headed it "Why Didn't He Get a Medal?"

The San Antonio Daily Light listed Decatur with Evansville, Terre Haute, Linton and Mount Vernon as signs of a movement in Indiana "against a race." A month later a Lincoln Independent columnist cited the one-dollar fine in a catalogue of lawlessness. All the coverage found was in white papers.

The Decatur wire and the local account placed the attack on Friday evening, July 3, while the Indianapolis Journal's editorial and its Decatur special said Saturday, the Fourth of July. The wire said Johnson was attacked while walking along the street; the more detailed local account said he was seized leaving a saloon. The mob numbered 100 by the wire and "fifty or more" by the Journal. The wire called Foreman the "leader of the mob," but the Journal's correspondent wrote that he "was not one of the ring leaders" and had been beaten by police.

reader.title: Expulsion of John Johnson from Decatur, Indiana
bases: A mob seized and chased a Black visitor and, despite the police, drove him from town, which the papers described as a negro 'run out' of Decatur where residents boasted no Black person could live (A13, A3, A1).

A wire dispatch (A3), the Indianapolis Journal's Decatur special (A10) and the local account reprinted in the Berne Witness (A13) agree that a mob attacked and drove out a Black man from Wren and that Will Foreman was fined one dollar.

accounts.label: Wire report (Decatur, July 6)
accounts.gist: A mob of 100 drove Johnson of Wren, O., from Decatur; he was walking along the street when attacked, and officers clubbed the mob, badly beating several citizens; the second race riot there in a year.

accounts.label: Local account (Decatur 'Journal', reprinted in the Berne Witness)
accounts.gist: A gang organized in a saloon grabbed the man as he left after buying drinks; Policeman Mangold clubbed one holder, and the man fled, was caught again in a clothing store, broke away and left by the Erie railroad with two policemen.

accounts.label: Wire report on the fine
accounts.gist: Will Foreman, 'leader of the mob', was fined $1 for assault and battery and no other arrests were made.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal special (Decatur, July 7)
accounts.gist: Foreman, the only person arrested, was fined $1 and $9.80 costs; he was not a ringleader but one of those beaten by police; citizens wanted Johnson to return and file riot affidavits.

framing.detail: Indianapolis Journal editorial 'Civilization in Decatur' called it 'a disgrace to our civilization' and urged state action as against 'whitecap outrages and lynchings'; its follow-up was headed 'A Travesty of Justice / Decatur Negro Baiter Is Fined One Dollar and Costs'.
The Berne Witness, headed 'Another Negro Run Down in Decatur', said the man 'offended no one' and printed the mayor's equal-rights reprimand.
The first wire, 'Some Good Citizens Have Headaches', called Johnson 'a respected citizen' while making light of the mob's beating by police.

The fine wire ran under 'Decatur, Ind., Has the Disease' (Montgomery), 'Indignation Increased' (Birmingham), 'Leader of a Negro Mob' (Oxford, Miss.), 'Mob Leader Fined $1' (Salt Lake, Beatrice) and 'Why Didn't He Get a Medal?' (Wisconsin).
San Antonio Daily Light named Decatur among Indiana towns in 'a general movement against the negroes' that was 'against a race'.
